item.title: More Mentions, Less Information? Diagnosing Identity and Alignment in Reddit Embeddings for Volatility Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.25468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since the 2021 GameStop short squeeze, r/WallStreetBets (WSB) has been associated with episodes of extreme volatility, and its text is increasingly used to forecast volatility. A model using only large language model (LLM) embeddings of WSB posts attains an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.13 for log realized variance. That number shows predictive power, but it does not reveal where the information comes from or how much the text adds beyond a firm's own volatility history. We answer these questions with a diagnostic protocol that nests embeddings on a heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) benchmark, compares them with text-free firm-identity controls, shuffles the day-to-text pairing within firm-years to test day-specific alignment, and checks whether gains persist across periods and coverage groups. We apply the protocol to frozen LLM embeddings in a panel of 202,145 mentioned stock-days, using retrospective rolling out-of-sample tests over 2015-2022. The results indicate that most of the standalone fit reflects firm or firm-year information: on firms seen in training, a text-free firm baseline reaches $R^2 = 0.32$, shuffling preserves 89-92% of the standalone fit, and masking ticker strings reduces standalone $R^2$ to -0.005. Adding embeddings to HAR reduces equal-date MSE by 1.22% (95% CI [0.94, 1.49]). This small but statistically significant gain survives firm controls and ticker masking, but is largely eliminated by alignment shuffling. The gain is concentrated in 2015-2019 and is not distinguishable from zero in 2020-2022. Expanding coverage by 48% through off-hours and weekend posts adds stock-days with no reliable positive increment. More mentions therefore do not imply more incremental forecasting information.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyu Zheng

item.title: Conflicting History in Foundation Model Return Forecasts
item.description: arXiv:2610.25822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Older observations can help a forecaster learn a predictive relationship while becoming misleading when that relationship changes. We study this tension using paired return histories that differ in older observations but share recent returns and the conditional distribution of the next return. Across five foundation-model forecasting procedures and three simulated processes, each evaluated on 1,024 independent replications, conflicting history reduces the probability of improving on zero in all 30 higher-signal comparisons. This loss of usefulness occurs despite successful signal recovery under stable conditions. A separate exploratory comparison on 56 assets finds that shortening inputs from 256 to 64 returns increases mean absolute error for every model by 1.77-4.58 basis points; neither length improves observed overall error over zero. The evidence distinguishes the ability to extract a signal from the ability to withstand conflicting history, while showing why context sensitivity alone does not justify discarding older data.
item.dc:creator: Levent Bulut

item.title: Amortized Neural Filtering for Calibrated Posteriors in Statistical Arbitrage
item.description: arXiv:2610.25802v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Statistical arbitrage trades on an estimate of the state of a residual spread, and conventional practice discards the uncertainty of that estimate. We keep the uncertainty and use it in the trading decision. A Neural Filter Estimator (NFE) is trained on simulated paths of a mean-reverting process whose innovation law is selected by testing candidates against real residuals; once trained, it returns the posterior over the latent state of every spread in a cross-section in one forward pass. Three results follow. On simulated paths with known truth, every practical estimator, ours included, falls in one narrow band of accuracy well below an estimator given full information, so the posterior gains no accuracy over a point estimate; its contribution is a correct account of its own uncertainty. On Korean equities, net of costs, the conventional point estimate forecasts about a thousand basis points per holding period more than it realizes, and the amortized methods cut that gap by a factor of roughly two to eight. Sizing positions from the posterior on the same learned factors as the end-to-end Attention Factor Model matches the Sharpe ratio of those factors under the base rule within the period's noise, at no more risk.
item.dc:creator: Minkey Chang

item.title: Probability-Weighting Functions for Normal Tempered-Stable Laws: Orthogonal Channels and Information-Theoretic Indices
item.description: arXiv:2610.26746v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A probability-weighting function (PWF) maps objective probabilities into decision weights. We construct PWFs from changes in the distribution of returns rather than from a parametric family: with prior and posterior return distributions $F_{prior}$ and $F_{post}$, the PWF is $w(p) = F_{post}(F_{prior}^{-1}(p))$. Both distributions are normal tempered-stable (NTS), and the posterior differs from the prior along one of three channels, each isolated with the variance held fixed: scale, skewness and tail thickness. Around a symmetric benchmark with excess kurtosis 3, a 40% change in scale moves cumulative probabilities by up to 7 to 8 percentage points, a skewness of $\pm 0.5$ by 2 percentage points, and a change of $\pm 0.3$ in the tail index by about 2 percentage points. The three channels leave distinct signatures: the deviation $w(p) - p$ changes sign once, twice and three times, respectively. Three information-theoretic indices (a Fisher-normalized logit shift, a signed Jensen-Shannon divergence and a log-odds elasticity) summarize the distortions and avoid the endpoint singularity of the classical ratio $(w(p)-p)/[p(1-p)]$. Applied to NTS parameters calibrated to S&P 500 ETF daily returns over 2015-2025, the same channels produce distortions of 2 to 7 percentage points. Code that reproduces every figure and number in the paper is provided.
item.dc:creator: Akash Deep, Bhathiya Divelgama, A. Alexandre Trindade, W. Brent Lindquist, Svetlozar T. Rachev, Frank J. Fabozzi

item.title: Market Efficiency in a Changing Asset Population: Mobility, Entry, and Survival over Cryptocurrency's Full History
item.description: arXiv:2610.23283v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Weak-form efficiency implies symmetry restrictions on the Markov chain governing movement across the cryptocurrency capitalisation distribution. We test them on the full listed population: 8,970 assets, 690 weekly cross-sections, 2013 to 2026, with entry, exit and survival observed rather than inferred. Symmetry is rejected in every era, but the asymmetry falls by seventy percent, and what converged is entry-driven compositional churn rather than coins' own valuations. The bottom decile earns 27.5% per week on paper and nothing among assets that trade, on capacity of $293,000. Compensation for neglect exists precisely where trading does not.
item.dc:creator: Antonis Ballis, Christos Ioannidis

item.title: Conditionally Identifiable Latent Representation for Multivariate Time Series with Structural Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2603.22886v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose the Identifiable Variational Dynamic Factor Model (iVDFM) for multivariate time series. The model combines variational inference with partial identifiability guarantees up to a known ambiguity class. Innovations follow a conditional exponential-family prior over observed auxiliary context and regime embeddings. Linear diagonal dynamics map innovations to factors and preserve that class, so factors are partially identifiable up to permutation and component-wise affine maps. We train by maximizing the ELBO and estimate uncertainty in both latent trajectories and forecasts. Under explicit assumptions, we prove partial identifiability up to the stated class and provide the full proof in the appendix. We evaluate factor recovery on synthetic DGPs, intervention behavior on synthetic SCMs, and forecasting on real benchmarks with CRPS and MSE.
item.dc:creator: Minkey Chang, Jae-Young Kim

item.title: Buy the Rumor, Sell the News: When Is News Priced In?
item.description: arXiv:2608.14014v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Two old market sayings hold that news is already priced in by the time it is published, and that the rumor is bought while the news is sold. Both are empirical claims about event time: they place the price move associated with a piece of news before and at publication rather than after it. Whether the claims hold, for which kinds of news, and by how much are basic questions about how fast markets absorb public information. We test them on 4.57 million financial news articles covering roughly 3,000 US stocks (2023-2026). A large language model teacher, distilled into a compact classifier through active learning, assigns each article one of 17 event tags and five attributes; articles are clustered into stories to separate first reports from follow-up coverage; and beta-adjusted abnormal returns are measured around the resulting 1.68 million stock-day events, with 364{,}405 neutral-sentiment events as a placebo group. Three results follow. First, the price move associated with news concentrates before and at publication: pooled across all signed events, the cumulative move in the news direction by the close of publication day is 2.8 times its value twenty days later, and for rumor-flagged events the directional return is concentrated around the rumor event, with little incremental return at the subsequent linked non-rumor event. Second, measured against the placebo of comparable stocks, markets underreact to numbers and overreact to stories: quantified fundamental news (earnings, dividends, guidance, analyst actions) keeps drifting in the direction of the news for weeks, while soft story-driven news (launches, macro commentary, leadership) gives back its move. Third, news carries width as well as direction: neutral news raises publication-day volatility. The study also produces a table of measured drift for each event tag, usable as a prior in news-conditioned forecasting models.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Kargarzadeh, Nariman Khaledian, Navid Parvini, Sid Ghatak, Arman Khaledian
